guide.see: Answer all five questions correctly and the first worlds in the Portal Hall open for building.
steps: Stand in front of the displays, facing them. A is on the left, D on the right.
For each display, compare the copy with the original. Was it just slid along? Turned around? Is it a mirror image? Or was every block sent through a centre point to the opposite side?
Press T, type /quiz and press Enter. Answer which move made each copy.
guide.title: Gallery 1: Four kinds of symmetry
guide.what: Each of the four displays, A to D, shows the same small shape twice: the original on the left, and on the right a copy made by one move.
guide.word: These moves are called symmetry operations: translation (slide), rotation (turn), reflection (mirror) and inversion (through a point).

0.hint: Is the copy the same way round as the original, or a mirror image of it?
0.q: Display A shows a shape and its copy. Which operation made the copy?
0.why: The copy is a mirror image: left and right are swapped, which no rotation can do.

0.hint: Walk around the display. Could you turn the original to match the copy without lifting it off the floor?
0.q: Display B: which operation made the copy?
0.why: The copy is the shape turned half a turn (180 degrees) about a vertical axis.

0.hint: Compare the two shapes: is anything turned or swapped, or is the copy just somewhere else?
0.q: Display C: which operation made the copy?
0.why: The copy is the same shape, the same way round, just moved along a line.

0.hint: Is the copy upside down? Which way does each part point compared with the original?
0.q: Display D: which operation made the copy?
0.why: Every block went through the centre point to the opposite side: up became down, east became west, north became south.

0.hint: Hold your hands up to a mirror. Which hand looks back at you?
0.q: Which operation turns a left hand into a right hand?
0.why: Reflection reverses handedness. Translations and rotations never do.

glossary: Symmetry operation: a move that leaves an object indistinguishable from how it started.
Symmetry element: the point, line or plane an operation acts about (centre, axis, mirror plane).
n-fold rotation axis: rotating by 360/n degrees leaves the object unchanged. Written n (2, 3, 4, 6).
Mirror plane: written m. It swaps left- and right-handed shapes.
Inversion centre: written -1 (say 'bar one'). Sends (x, y, z) to (-x, -y, -z).
Rotoinversion: a rotation followed by an inversion, written -n (-1, -3, -4, -6). A mirror is the same as -2.
Point group: the set of all symmetry operations of an object that leave one point fixed.
Order of a group: how many operations it contains. One block in a general position makes that many copies.
Hermann-Mauguin symbol: the standard short name of a group, such as 4mm or 2/m. '/' means 'with a mirror perpendicular to'.
Lattice: an infinite array of points, each with identical surroundings. A crystal is a motif repeated on a lattice.
Unit cell: the repeating box of a crystal. Copying it along the lattice translations fills space.
Screw axis: rotate, then translate along the axis. 2_1 means a half turn plus half a cell.
Glide plane: reflect, then translate parallel to the plane by a fraction of a lattice translation, usually half a cell edge.
Crystallographic restriction: a lattice can only have 1-, 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold rotation axes. 5-fold and 7-fold or higher are impossible in a periodic crystal.
There are exactly 32 crystallographic point groups. 25 of them fit a cubic block grid; the 7 hexagonal ones need a 6-fold or -6 axis, which a square grid does not have.
Plane group: the symmetry of a repeating pattern on a flat surface, such as a tiled floor. There are exactly 17. 12 of them fit a square block grid; the other 5 need 3-fold or 6-fold rotations.
Chiral: a shape that cannot be moved to match its own mirror image, like a hand. An achiral shape has a mirror plane or an inversion centre of its own.
Quasicrystals (discovered by Dan Shechtman, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2011) show 5-fold symmetry in diffraction because they are ordered but not periodic.
intro: Welcome to the Museum of Crystals and Symmetry!
Start in the foyer (type /spawn to go there): read the big board, then walk through the door into Gallery 1.
Walk with W A S D, look with the mouse. Press T to type a command, such as /tour for a ten-minute guided tour.

1: A mirror plane (m) runs through the middle of this plaza, north to south.
Everything you build is reflected to the other side.
Task: build half a butterfly or a letter, and watch the mirror finish it.
Notice: build a shape that points left, and its image points right. A mirror swaps handedness.
3: A mirror is the same as a 2-fold rotation followed by an inversion, so it is also written -2.
Like inversion, a mirror is an 'improper' operation: no way of moving a solid object through space can produce it.

guide.example: A methanol molecule (CH3OH) has one mirror plane and no other symmetry: point group m (chemists write Cs).
guide.see: Every block gets one copy at the same distance on the other side, so 2 blocks for each one you place. Build an F and its copy is a backwards F. A block right in the sheet of dots is its own reflection, so it stays single.
steps: Walk through the gate onto the square. A sheet of light-blue dots in the air shows where the mirror is.
Stand on one side of the sheet and place a block on the ground.
Now build half of something: half a butterfly, half a heart, or the letter F.
guide.title: Mirror Plaza
guide.what: An invisible mirror stands across the middle of this square, running north to south. It copies everything you build onto the other side.
guide.word: The mirror is called a mirror plane, written m. A mirror swaps left and right.

1.q: You place one block next to the mirror plane, not on it. How many blocks appear in total, counting yours?
1.why: The group m has 2 operations: do nothing, and reflect. So a block off the plane gives 2.

1.q: You place a block exactly on the mirror plane. How many blocks appear?
1.why: A block on the plane is its own mirror image.

3.q: A mirror plane is the same as which rotoinversion?
3.why: Rotating 180 degrees and then inverting through a point on the axis gives a reflection in the plane perpendicular to that axis: m = -2.

showcase.text: Half a butterfly was built west of the mirror; the mirror made the other wing.

1: A 2-fold rotation axis stands upright in the middle of this yard.
Each block is copied half a turn (180 degrees) around it.
Task: build one blade of a propeller and watch the second appear.
Notice: a rotation never turns a left hand into a right hand.

guide.example: A hydrogen peroxide molecule (H2O2) has only a 2-fold axis: point group 2 (chemists write C2).
guide.see: Each block gets one copy on the exact opposite side of the pole: 2 blocks for each one. The copy is turned around, but it is not a mirror image: walk around it and it matches.
steps: Find the middle of the yard: yellow lens shapes, like lemons, float one above the other there. They mark the pole.
Place a block a few steps away from the pole.
Build one blade of a propeller: a line of blocks reaching out from the pole.
guide.title: Twofold Yard
guide.what: An invisible pole stands upright in the middle of this yard. Everything you build is copied half a turn around the pole, to its opposite side.
guide.word: A half-turn symmetry is called a 2-fold rotation axis, written 2: two half turns make a full turn.

1.q: How many times must you apply a half turn to get back to where you started?
1.why: Two half turns make one full turn. That is why it is called 2-fold.

showcase.text: One propeller blade was built; the 2-fold axis added the second, half a turn round.

1: A 4-fold rotation axis stands upright in the middle of this tower.
Each block is copied a quarter turn (90 degrees) at a time around it.
Task: build a windmill with four blades by building just one.
An n-fold axis turns by 360/n degrees; doing it n times brings you back to the start.

guide.example: Crystals with only a 4-fold axis are rare. Pinnoite, a borate mineral, is one: its crystal class is 4.
guide.see: Each block appears 4 times, a quarter turn apart, like the four sails of a windmill. Blocks built right on the pole are not copied, because turning leaves them where they are.
steps: Go into the tower and find the middle: red squares float one above the other there. They mark the pole.
Place one block on the floor a few steps away from the pole, and count the blocks.
Now make a windmill: build a post straight up from the middle, then one sail sticking out sideways from its top.
guide.title: Fourfold Tower
guide.what: An invisible pole stands upright in the middle of this tower. Everything you build is copied a quarter turn around the pole, again and again, so every block appears in four places.
guide.word: This is a 4-fold rotation axis, written 4: four quarter turns make one full turn.

1.q: You place one block away from the axis. How many blocks appear in total, counting yours?
1.why: The group 4 has 4 operations: turns of 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees.

1.q: Which rotation is hidden inside a 4-fold axis?
1.why: Two quarter turns make a half turn, so every 4-fold axis is also a 2-fold axis.

showcase.text: One windmill sail was built; the 4-fold axis added the other three.

1: An inversion centre (-1, say 'bar one') floats in the middle of this cube.
Each block is sent straight through the centre to the same distance on the other side.
Fly in (press K to fly). Right-click with a block while pointing at nothing to place it 3 blocks in front of you.
Build near a corner: the copy appears at the opposite corner, upside down.
In coordinates: (x, y, z) becomes (-x, -y, -z).

guide.example: Kyanite, a blue mineral, has only an inversion centre: its crystal class is -1.
guide.see: The copy is upside down and back to front at the same time: up became down, east became west and north became south. Each block gives 2. A white disc marks the centre point.
steps: Press K to fly, then fly into the cube. Hold Space to rise and Shift to sink.
To place a block in mid-air, point at empty space and right-click: it appears 3 steps in front of you.
Build a small shape near one corner of the cube, then fly to the opposite corner.
guide.title: Inversion Core
guide.what: An invisible point floats in the middle of this big cube. Every block you build is sent straight through that point to the other side, the same distance away.
guide.word: This is an inversion centre, written -1 (say 'bar one').

1.q: A block sits 3 blocks above and 2 blocks east of the centre. Where is its copy?
1.why: Inversion reverses every direction: above becomes below and east becomes west.

1.q: Does inversion turn a left hand into a right hand?
1.why: Yes. Like a mirror, inversion is an improper operation and reverses handedness.

showcase.text: A blue corner with three arms was built near the bottom; inversion put an upside-down copy at the opposite corner.

1: This hall is a crystal: 27 identical boxes (unit cells) stacked 3 by 3 by 3.
Build anything in one box and it is copied into every box.
A crystal is a motif (your build) repeated on a lattice (the grid of boxes).
The moves from one box to the next are translations.
4: The box is the unit cell; its edge lengths are the lattice parameters (here 8 blocks each way).
A real crystal repeats its unit cell billions of times in every direction.
Only lattice translations are imposed here, so the space group is P1.

guide.example: A grain of table salt is one tiny unit cell repeated by translations like these in all three directions.
guide.see: Your object appears 27 times, once in each box, always the same way round. Nothing is turned or mirrored: each copy is only slid along.
steps: Press K to fly and go in. Orange lines mark the edges of the boxes.
Choose one box and build a small object in it.
Fly back and look along the rows of boxes.
guide.title: Translation Hall
guide.what: This hall works like a crystal. It is divided into 27 identical boxes, 3 by 3 by 3, each 8 blocks wide. Whatever you build in one box is copied into every other box.
guide.word: Each box is a unit cell, and the slides are translations. A real crystal repeats its unit cell billions of times in every direction.

1.q: You place one block. How many blocks appear in the hall?
1.why: One copy in each of the 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 unit cells.

showcase.text: One cell got a red block at its corner and a blue one at its centre; the lattice repeated them. Caesium chloride is built this way: one kind of ion at the cell corners, the other at the cell centre.

2: Two mirror planes meet at right angles along the vertical line in the middle.
Build one block and look closely: there are four blocks, but only two mirrors.
Two mirrors at an angle make a rotation by twice that angle. 2 x 90 = 180 degrees, so a 2-fold axis appears where they meet.
The name mm2 lists the two mirrors and the 2-fold axis they create.

guide.example: A water molecule (H2O) has the symmetry of this square: point group mm2 (chemists write C2v).
guide.see: There are 4 blocks: one in each quarter. Two of them are reflections in the two mirrors. The fourth, in the opposite quarter, is your block turned half a turn about the line where the mirrors cross: two mirrors together make a turn.
steps: Find the two sheets of light-blue dots that cross in the middle.
Place one block in one of the four quarters, away from both sheets.
Count the blocks and look at where each one is.
guide.title: Twin Mirrors
guide.what: Two invisible mirrors cross in the middle of this square: one runs north to south, the other east to west.
guide.word: The name mm2 means: a mirror, another mirror, and the 2-fold axis they create.

2.q: How many copies does one block off the mirrors make, counting yours?
2.why: mm2 has 4 operations: nothing, mirror 1, mirror 2, and the 2-fold rotation.

2.q: Two mirror planes meet at 45 degrees. What rotation do they create?
2.why: Twice the angle: 2 x 45 = 90 degrees, a 4-fold rotation.

showcase.text: One green seat was built; two mirrors made four.

2: A vertical 2-fold axis, plus a horizontal mirror plane perpendicular to it.
'/' in the name means 'with a mirror perpendicular to', so 2/m reads 'two over m'.
Combine the two and a third operation appears for free: an inversion centre where axis and mirror meet.
Task: build near a top corner and find the copy at the opposite bottom corner.

guide.example: Gypsum, the mineral used to make plaster, forms monoclinic crystals of class 2/m.
guide.see: 4 blocks for each one you place. The fourth copy is at the opposite bottom corner: your shape sent through the centre point. A half turn plus a mirror across it creates an inversion centre.
steps: Press K to fly and go in.
Build a small shape near one of the top corners.
Find its copies: one half a turn round the pole, one reflected in the flat mirror below it, and one more.
guide.title: Monoclinic Cube
guide.what: In this cube, an invisible pole stands upright through the middle, and a flat mirror lies across the middle like a glass floor.
guide.word: 2/m (say 'two over m'): a 2-fold axis with a mirror perpendicular to it.

2.q: Which extra operation do a 2-fold axis and a perpendicular mirror create together?
2.why: Half turn about z: (x,y,z) -> (-x,-y,z). Then mirror: z -> -z. Together: (-x,-y,-z), an inversion.
Identity, the 2-fold rotation, the mirror, and the inversion.

showcase.text: One purple hook was built; the axis, the mirror and the inversion centre they make gave four.

2: A 4-fold axis with mirror planes: two along the sides and two along the diagonals.
The region was given one 4-fold axis and one mirror; combining them produces four mirrors.
This is the symmetry of a square seen from above.

guide.example: A bromine pentafluoride molecule (BrF5) is a square pyramid: point group 4mm (chemists write C4v).
guide.see: Each block appears 8 times: 4 by turning, and each of those mirrored. It is the symmetry of a square tile seen from above.
steps: Find the middle (red squares) and the four sheets of light-blue dots.
Place one block a few steps from the middle, but not in a sheet of dots.
Count the blocks, then build a small shape and watch the pattern.
guide.title: Square Court
guide.what: An invisible quarter-turn pole stands in the middle of this square, and four mirrors pass through it: two parallel to the sides and two along the diagonals.
guide.word: 4mm: a 4-fold axis and two kinds of mirror.

2.q: How many copies does one block in a general position make, counting yours?
How many mirror planes does 4mm have?
2.why: Turning the side mirror by 90 degrees gives a second side mirror, and combining a mirror with a quarter turn gives the two diagonal mirrors: 2 + 2 = 4.

showcase.text: One petal was laid on the floor; four mirrors and the 4-fold axis made a flower of eight.

2: Three mirror planes, all at right angles, each through the middle of a shoebox and parallel to one pair of its faces.
Each pair of mirrors makes a 2-fold axis, and all three together make an inversion centre.
The full name is 2/m 2/m 2/m; mmm is the short form.

guide.example: Olivine, a green mineral common in the Earth's mantle, forms orthorhombic crystals of class mmm.
guide.see: The three mirrors cut the cube into 8 corner pieces, and your shape appears once in each: 8 blocks for each one you place. Neighbouring copies are mirror images of each other.
steps: Press K to fly and go in.
Build a small shape near one corner of the cube.
Visit the other corners.
guide.title: Orthorhombic Cube
guide.what: Three invisible mirrors meet in the middle of this cube, all at right angles: one north to south, one east to west, and one lying flat.
guide.word: mmm: three mirrors. Every two of them also make a 2-fold axis, and all three make an inversion centre.

2.q: How many operations does mmm have?
2.why: Identity, 3 mirrors, 3 two-fold rotations and the inversion: 8.

showcase.text: One orange hook was built; three mirrors made eight.

3: A 3-fold axis runs along the long diagonal of this cube, from one corner to the opposite corner.
It turns the cube by 120 degrees: east goes to north, north goes to up, and up goes to east.
In coordinates it just cycles them: (x, y, z) -> (z, x, y).
A cube has four such diagonals, which is what makes cubic crystals special.

guide.example: A methane molecule (CH4) has four 3-fold axes: look down any C-H bond, and a third of a turn swaps the other three H atoms.
guide.see: Your line appears 3 times: once pointing east, once pointing north and once pointing up. A third of a turn about the diagonal swaps the three directions round.
steps: Press K to fly and go in. Green triangles mark the diagonal pole.
Build a short line of blocks pointing east, away from the diagonal.
Look for the other two copies of your line.
guide.title: Diagonal Cube
guide.what: An invisible pole runs through this cube from one corner to the opposite corner, along its longest diagonal. Each copy is turned one third of a turn about it.
guide.word: A 3-fold rotation axis, written 3. A cube has four of these diagonals.

3.q: How many copies does one block off the diagonal make, counting yours?

showcase.text: A cyan hook was built off the diagonal and made three; the white block sits on the 3-fold axis and stays single.

3: -4 (say 'bar four'): turn a quarter turn about the vertical axis, then invert through the centre.
Neither step alone is a symmetry here; only the combination is.
Doing it twice gives a plain half turn, so -4 contains a 2-fold axis but no 4-fold axis and no inversion centre.

guide.example: Chalcopyrite, a brassy copper ore, has crystal class -42m, which contains a -4 axis.
guide.see: Each block appears 4 times, a quarter turn apart, and they take turns: above, below, above, below. A plain quarter turn alone would not make this pattern.
steps: Press K to fly and go in.
Build a small shape in the upper half of the room, away from the middle.
Look for the copies all the way round the middle, above and below.
guide.title: Rotoinversion Room
guide.what: The move here has two steps: turn a quarter turn about the upright pole in the middle, then send the block through the centre point to the other side.
guide.word: -4 (say 'bar four') is a rotoinversion. Doing it twice gives a plain half turn, so -4 contains a 2-fold axis.

3.q: Which of these does the group -4 contain?
3.why: (-4)^2 = a half turn. The 4-fold rotation and the inversion only occur together, never separately.

showcase.text: One magenta hook was built; -4 made four, alternately up and down.

3: -3 (say 'bar three'): turn a third of a turn about the long diagonal of the cube, then invert through the centre.
Doing it twice gives a plain 3-fold rotation, and doing it three times gives the inversion itself.
So -3 contains both a 3-fold axis and an inversion centre. Compare the Rotoinversion Room: -4 contains neither a 4-fold axis nor an inversion centre.
Calcite, the mineral of limestone and marble, has a -3 axis: its point group is -3m.

guide.example: Dolomite, a carbonate mineral like calcite, has crystal class -3: a 3-fold axis and an inversion centre, but no mirrors.
guide.see: Each block appears 6 times: 3 by the thirds of a turn, and each of those sent through the centre. Here, unlike in the Rotoinversion Room, the plain turn and the plain trip through the centre are symmetries too.
steps: Press K to fly and go in.
Build a small shape a few blocks away from one corner.
Look for its copies near the other corners.
guide.title: Bar-Three Room
guide.what: Two steps again: turn one third of a turn about the long diagonal of the room, then send the block through the centre point.
guide.word: -3 (say 'bar three'). Calcite, the mineral in marble, has it.

options: A 3-fold axis and an inversion centre
3.q: Which of these does the group -3 contain?
3.why: (-3) twice is a 3-fold rotation and (-3) three times is the inversion, so both are in the group. It has 6 operations.

3.q: You place one block off the diagonal and away from the centre. How many blocks appear in total?
3.why: -3 has 6 operations: the identity, two 3-fold rotations, the inversion and two -3 rotoinversions.

showcase.text: One green hook was built; -3 made six around the diagonal.

3: The full symmetry of a cube: m-3m, the highest point symmetry a crystal can have.
3 four-fold axes, 4 three-fold axes, 6 two-fold axes, 9 mirrors and an inversion centre.
Place one block anywhere off the symmetry elements and it becomes 48.
Metals such as copper, iron and aluminium have this symmetry.

guide.example: Halite (rock salt) crystals have class m-3m and usually grow as cubes.
guide.see: One block becomes 48. A few blocks become a star.
steps: Press K to fly and go in.
Place one block anywhere that is not in the middle and not on a marker.
Then add two or three more blocks next to it.
guide.title: Kaleidoscope
guide.what: This cube has the full symmetry of a cube: every way of turning a cube so that it still fits its box, and the mirror image of each.
guide.word: m-3m: the highest symmetry a crystal can have. Copper, iron and table salt have it.

3.q: How many operations does m-3m have?
3.why: 48: the 24 rotations of a cube, and each of those combined with inversion.

showcase.text: Three blocks were placed: yellow off every element (48 copies), green on a 3-fold axis (8, the corners of a cube) and red on a 4-fold axis (6, the corners of an octahedron).

3: This room was meant to have a 6-fold axis. It cannot be built on a block grid.
Turn a square grid by 60 degrees and the grid points no longer land on grid points.
Every operation that maps the block grid onto itself just permutes x, y and z and flips signs; none of these is a 6-fold rotation.
So only 25 of the 32 crystal point groups fit here. The 7 hexagonal ones need a hexagonal lattice, like graphite or snowflakes.
No lattice at all allows a 5-fold axis: that is the crystallographic restriction.

guide.example: Snowflakes have six-fold symmetry because ice crystals are hexagonal: a grid that square blocks cannot make.
guide.see: Square blocks allow half turns and quarter turns, and thirds of a turn about a cube's diagonal, but never sixths. Six-fold symmetry needs a grid of hexagons, like a honeycomb.
steps: Place a block: no copies appear, because 1 block stays 1.
Look at the floor grid and imagine turning it by one sixth of a turn (60 degrees): the corners of the blocks no longer land on the grid.
guide.title: Impossible Room
guide.what: This room was meant to have a six-fold pole: one sixth of a turn. That cannot work in a world made of square blocks, so the room copies nothing.
guide.word: The crystallographic restriction: a crystal can only have 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold rotations, never 5-fold.

3.q: Which rotation axes can a periodic crystal have?
3.why: Rotations must map lattice points to lattice points. That only allows 1-, 2-, 3-, 4- and 6-fold axes.

4: A 2_1 screw axis: turn half a turn about a vertical axis, then rise by half a unit cell.
Build a block and follow its copies upward: they spiral like a staircase.
A screw axis needs a repeating translation, so it occurs in periodic structures such as crystals, never in the symmetry of a single finite object.

guide.example: Sugar (sucrose) crystals have space group P2_1, like this hall. About 30% of protein crystals have P2_1 2_1 2_1: three 2_1 axes.
guide.see: In each column your shape swaps sides as it climbs: turn and rise, turn and rise. 2 copies in every box, 54 in all.
steps: Press K to fly and go in. The hall is divided into 27 boxes, 3 by 3 by 3, each 6 blocks wide.
Build a small shape low down in one box.
Follow its copies upward.
guide.title: Screw Hall
guide.what: Here the copies climb like steps of a staircase: each one is turned half a turn and lifted half a box higher.
guide.word: A 2_1 screw axis (say 'two-one'). Screw axes exist only in crystals, because they need a pattern that repeats.

options: A shift of one whole cell upward
4.q: Apply the 2_1 screw operation twice. What do you get?
4.why: Two half turns make a full turn, and two half-cell rises make one full cell: a lattice translation.

4.q: Can a single, finite object, like a vase, have a 2_1 screw axis?
4.why: No. A screw includes a shift, and a finite object cannot be shifted onto itself. Screw axes need a repeating structure.

showcase.text: One orange step was built; the 2_1 screw axis turned it and lifted it, making a spiral staircase.

4: A glide plane: reflect in a vertical plane, then slide half a cell along it.
Like footprints in snow: left, right, left, right, each one a mirror image moved forward.

guide.example: Footprints left by someone walking on a beach repeat by a glide: each print is the mirror image of the last, moved forward.
guide.see: Your arrow repeats in a zig-zag, left side, right side, left side, each a mirror image of the one before and 3 blocks further east. 2 in every box, 32 in all.
steps: The hall is a floor of 16 boxes, 4 by 4, each 6 blocks wide and 6 high.
Build an arrow pointing east in one box.
Walk east along the row and watch the arrows.
guide.title: Glide Hall
guide.what: Here the copies are like footprints in snow: each one is mirrored, then slid half a box forward.
guide.word: A glide plane: a mirror and a slide along it, together.

options: A translation parallel to the plane
4.q: A glide reflection is a reflection combined with what?
4.why: The slide is half a lattice translation, parallel to the mirror plane.

options: A shift of one whole cell along the plane
4.q: Apply the glide twice. What do you get?
4.why: Two reflections cancel, and two half-cell slides make a whole cell: a lattice translation.

showcase.text: One footprint was built; the glide plane made a trail of left and right prints.

4: A 4_1 screw axis: a quarter turn about the vertical axis, then a rise of a quarter of a cell (here 2 blocks).
Four steps make one full turn and one full cell, so the copies climb like a spiral staircase.
Its mirror image turns the other way, and is called 4_3. Screw axes can give crystals a handedness:
quartz has 3-fold screw axes (3_1 or 3_2), which is why there are left- and right-handed quartz crystals.
Try /step here to see each turn-and-rise named, or /byhand to place the steps yourself.

guide.example: Egg-white lysozyme, a protein, forms tetragonal crystals with space group P4_3 2_1 2. A 4_3 axis is the mirror twin of 4_1.
guide.see: After four quarter turns a copy is right above your step again, 8 blocks higher. 48 copies in all.
steps: Press K to fly and go in.
Near the bottom, beside the middle, build one step: a short line of 2 or 3 blocks.
Watch the steps climb.
guide.title: Spiral Tower
guide.what: Here the copies climb round the middle of the tower like a spiral staircase: each one turned a quarter turn and lifted 2 blocks.
guide.word: A 4_1 screw axis (say 'four-one'). Its mirror image turns the other way. Quartz comes in left- and right-handed crystals, whose atoms spiral opposite ways: 3_1 and 3_2 screw axes.

4.q: How many 4_1 steps bring a block back directly above where it started, exactly one cell higher?
4.why: Four quarter turns make one full turn, and four quarter-cell rises make one whole cell.

options: A 4_3 screw axis, turning the other way
4.q: What is the mirror image of a 4_1 screw axis?
4.why: A mirror reverses the sense of the turn but not the rise, so the right-handed 4_1 staircase becomes the left-handed 4_3.

showcase.text: One step was built; the 4_1 screw axis turned and lifted it into a spiral staircase, one quarter turn and two blocks up at a time.

4: This lab has a hidden symmetry. Build, look at the copies, and work out the point group.
Tip: build near the centre first, then far from it. Look for axes, mirrors and an inversion centre.

guide.see: The number of copies of one block tells you how many symmetry moves there are.
steps: Press K to fly and go in.
Place one block away from the middle and count all its copies.
Look at the copies: are any of them mirror images? Is one straight through the centre point? Is one above or below yours?
Type /quiz to name the symmetry.
guide.title: Mystery Lab
guide.what: This lab has a symmetry that is kept secret. Your job is to find out what it is.
guide.word: Point group: the full set of symmetry moves of an object.

4.q: What is the point group of the Mystery Lab?
4.why: A vertical 4-fold axis with a horizontal mirror perpendicular to it: 4/m. It also has an inversion centre.

options: Two more mirrors and two more 2-fold axes
4.q: A build has symmetry mmm. Which operations does it have that a 2/m build lacks?
4.why: 2/m has one 2-fold axis, one mirror and an inversion centre. mmm has three of each kind of axis and mirror, plus the inversion centre.

challenges.text: Build something whose symmetry is exactly 2/m, not mmm.
Build something with exactly 4mm symmetry: a 4-fold axis and mirrors, but nothing upside down.
Hard: build something with a -4 axis but no 4-fold axis.
Build something with the full symmetry of a cube.

4: Your lab. Build anything, then type /whatsymmetry to have the exact point group worked out.
Type /symmetry followed by a description (for example: a fourfold axis with mirrors) to give the lab that symmetry.
Try asking for a sixfold axis and see what happens.
Challenges: type /challenge to get a target symmetry, build it, then check it with /whatsymmetry.

guide.example: Mineralogists name a crystal's class the same way: by finding which symmetry moves its shape has.
guide.see: /whatsymmetry tests your build against all 48 ways the block grid can be turned and mirrored.
steps: Build anything, then type /whatsymmetry to find out the symmetry of what you built.
Type /symmetry 4mm (or another symbol you have learned) to give the lab that symmetry, then build again.
Try /symmetry 6 and read why it is refused. Type /challenge for a target to build.
guide.title: Free Lab
guide.what: Your own lab. It starts with no symmetry at all, so 1 block stays 1: you decide what happens.
guide.word: Every crystal has one of 32 point groups. 25 of them fit this block world.

4: A floor pattern with plane group pmm: mirror lines in two directions at right angles, repeated in every cell.
Place blocks on the floor and the pattern tiles the whole garden. Where two mirror lines cross, there is a 2-fold rotation point.
A plane group is the symmetry of a repeating flat pattern. There are exactly 17; this garden shows four.

guide.example: Bricks stacked in a plain grid, with no offset between rows (stack bond), have plane group pmm.
guide.see: Each block appears 4 times in every tile, and the tiles repeat over the floor: 144 blocks for one. Where two mirror lines cross, the pattern also has a half-turn point.
steps: Walk onto the garden floor. The floor colour changes from square to square: each square is one tile, 6 blocks wide.
Place blocks on the floor inside one tile.
Watch the pattern spread over the whole garden.
guide.title: Mirror Tiles
guide.what: The floor here is a repeating tile pattern, like a bathroom floor, with mirror lines in two directions.
guide.word: A plane group is the symmetry of a flat repeating pattern. pmm: mirrors in two directions. There are exactly 17 plane groups.

4.q: One block in a general position: how many copies appear in each unit cell, counting yours?
4.why: pmm has 4 operations per cell: the identity, two mirrors and the 2-fold rotation where they cross.

4.q: Of the 17 plane groups, how many can be built on a square block grid?
4.why: 12. The other 5 need 3-fold or 6-fold rotations, and turning a square grid by 120 or 60 degrees moves grid points off the grid.

showcase.text: One red hook per cell was placed; the mirror lines tiled the floor.

4: Plane group pgg: glide lines in two directions and 2-fold rotation points, but no mirror lines at all.
Each copy is either turned half a turn, or reflected and slid half a cell along the glide line.
Build an arrow on the floor and follow its copies: they alternate like footprints.

guide.example: A herringbone floor of identical wooden blocks has plane group pgg.
guide.see: Some arrows are turned half a turn; the others are mirror images that are also slid half a tile, so no arrow is a plain reflection of a neighbour. 144 blocks for one.
steps: Walk onto the garden floor (each tile is 6 blocks wide).
Build an arrow on the floor inside one tile.
Follow the copies of your arrow.
guide.title: Glide Tiles
guide.what: A repeating floor pattern with half-turn points and glides, but no plain mirrors.
guide.word: pgg: glides in two directions and half-turn points.

4.q: Does pgg have any mirror lines?
4.why: Every reflection in pgg comes with a slide of half a cell, so each one is a glide, never a plain mirror.

showcase.text: One cyan arrow was placed; turns and glides tiled the floor.

4: Plane group p4: 4-fold rotation points, repeated in every cell, and no mirrors or glides.
Without mirrors the pattern has a handedness: it turns one way, like a pinwheel, and its mirror image turns the other way.

guide.example: The pinwheel tiling of big and small squares, often used for floors, has plane group p4. It is chiral.
guide.see: The pattern spins one way, like a pinwheel; its mirror image would spin the other way. 144 blocks for one.
steps: Walk onto the garden floor (each tile is 6 blocks wide).
Build a short bent line on the floor inside one tile.
Look at the pattern from above (press K, fly up).
guide.title: Pinwheel Tiles
guide.what: A repeating floor pattern with quarter-turn points and no mirrors at all.
guide.word: p4: quarter-turn points only.

4.q: One block in a general position: how many copies appear in each unit cell, counting yours?
4.why: p4 has 4 operations per cell: turns of 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees.

showcase.text: One purple hook was placed; the 4-fold points turned it into pinwheels.

4: Plane group p4g: 4-fold rotation points with mirror lines and glide lines, but no mirror passes through a 4-fold point.
Compare it with Pinwheel Tiles next door: the extra glides and mirrors double the number of copies.

guide.example: M. C. Escher's drawing of angels and devils (sketch no. 45) has plane group p4g.
guide.see: Twice as many copies as in Pinwheel Tiles: 288 blocks for one. The extra mirrors and glides make the pattern look woven.
steps: Walk onto the garden floor (each tile is 6 blocks wide).
Build a short bent line on the floor inside one tile.
Compare it with Pinwheel Tiles.
guide.title: Weave Tiles
guide.what: A repeating floor pattern with quarter-turn points, mirrors and glides; but no mirror passes through a quarter-turn point.
guide.word: p4g: quarter turns plus mirrors and glides.

4.q: One block in a general position: how many copies appear in each unit cell, counting yours?
4.why: p4g has 8 operations per cell: the 4 rotations of p4, each combined with a reflection or glide.

showcase.text: The same hook as next door was placed; the extra mirrors and glides of p4g weave it into a different pattern.
